page: Microsoft Azure FX96-48ms_v2 is a compute-focused yet heavily memory-dense virtual machine powered by the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor. The instance is built on the x86_64 architecture using dedicated Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C processors operating at clock speeds up to 4.2 GHz. The allocation provides 48 vCPUs mapped across 24 physical cores at 2 threads per core, backed by 48 KB L1 data cache per core, 2 MB L2 cache per core, and a massive 260 MB shared L3 cache. Modern vector and matrix instruction extensions are fully supported, including AVX-512, AVX-VNNI, and Intel AMX (Advanced Matrix Extensions) for tile and int8 operations.

Hardware capacity highlights an atypical ratio of compute to memory, packing 1832.0 GB of RAM alongside its 48 vCPUs. This configuration yields approximately 38.17 GB of RAM per vCPU, placing it among the highest memory footprints in high-frequency compute classes. The instance does not feature bundled local storage or integrated GPUs, necessitating reliance on network-attached storage solutions. This setup keeps the instance tightly focused on purely in-memory data processing, caching, and CPU-driven mathematical execution.

Benchmark outcomes show top-tier execution across single-threaded and integer workloads, recording a Geekbench single-core score of 2341.0 and a multi-core score of 20535.0. Memory bandwidth testing shows high throughput, reaching 4135.8 GB/sec in small block read benchmarks and uncached large block transfers exceeding 332 GB/sec for reads and 158 GB/sec for writes. PassMark metrics confirm strong performance across extended instruction sets (75439.45) and encryption (56173.89), alongside 74.96 million operations per second on Redis SET evaluations.

The qualitative profile of the FX96-48ms_v2 balances substantial memory density with high per-core performance. While instances with constrained core counts relative to RAM capacity may show average throughput in total multi-core stress testing compared to instances with higher overall core numbers, the sheer scale of RAM paired with 4.2 GHz base frequencies delivers significant advantages for memory-constrained workflows. Suitable applications include massive in-memory databases, electronic design automation (EDA), complex financial modeling, compilation tasks, and CPU-based matrix inference workloads.
